title: Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics
answer: Polygenic risk, gene editing design, pharmacogenomics, epigenetic age and rare disease diagnosis.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Polygenic Risk Scores
children.blurb: Polygenic risk scores estimate a person's likelihood of developing a particular disease by adding up the small effects of many common genetic variants.

children.name: Gene Editing Guide Design
children.blurb: Gene editing guide design is the computational task of choosing short RNA sequences that direct a CRISPR-associated nuclease to a target DNA site while minimizing off-target cleavage and maximizing on-target efficiency.

children.name: Pharmacogenomics
children.blurb: Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation affects drug response, including efficacy, dosing, and adverse reactions.

children.name: Epigenetic Aging Clocks
children.blurb: Epigenetic aging clocks are computational models that estimate a person's biological age from patterns of DNA methylation, often differing from chronological age.

children.name: Rare Disease Diagnosis
children.blurb: Rare disease diagnosis uses AI to search genomic sequences, clinical notes, and phenotype descriptions for patterns that match known rare conditions.

sections.body: Genomic medicine and precision therapeutics use AI to interpret DNA, RNA, and other molecular data to guide care. Current work includes calculating polygenic risk scores that sum many small genetic effects, designing guide RNAs for CRISPR editing, predicting drug response from genetic variants, estimating biological age from DNA methylation, and ranking candidate genes for rare diseases. These are not hypothetical systems, they run on real patient sequence data in clinical and research labs. The AI does pattern matching and prediction, not independent biological discovery. It narrows search spaces and scores possibilities, but a human clinician or researcher still interprets the result.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field has solved some narrow tasks, like calling variants from sequencing reads and predicting whether a guide RNA is likely to cut at an off-target site. Polygenic risk scores are reproducible across populations of similar ancestry but degrade sharply when applied to people from different backgrounds. Pharmacogenomic models can flag a handful of well studied gene drug pairs, yet most medications still lack reliable genetic predictors. Epigenetic aging clocks produce a number that correlates with chronological age, but the biological meaning of that number is contested and it is not a diagnostic. Rare disease diagnosis has improved with AI ranking of candidate variants, but many patients remain undiagnosed because the causal variant is noncoding or the model lacks training data. Across the 1000 medical AI models tracked on this site, genomic tools are a small fraction and few have passed prospective clinical trials.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader wanting to understand how many small genetic effects are combined into one score should start with Polygenic Risk Scores. Gene Editing Guide Design explains the AI that chooses where CRISPR should cut and what off target effects to expect. Pharmacogenomics covers the link between genetic variants and drug metabolism or response, which is the most clinically used part of this section. Epigenetic Aging Clocks describes models that estimate age from methylation patterns and the debate over what that estimate means. Rare Disease Diagnosis walks through how AI ranks candidate genes and variants for patients with unexplained conditions, and where those rankings still fail. Together these pages move from population level risk to single patient molecular interpretation, but each page stands alone for a specific question.
